faqs.q: How do I know if the droppings in my East Orange basement are from rats?
faqs.a: Rat droppings are capsule-shaped and about half an inch long — much larger than mouse droppings — and they concentrate along walls, near food storage, and beside the grease-dark rub marks rats leave on the routes they run nightly. In East Orange apartment basements the droppings concentrate by the boiler rooms and the old coal bins, and the rub marks on the pipe runs show exactly which buildings on the block are connected by travel routes. A rat job here is three parts: trapping out the animals present, sealing the entries (a rat needs only a half-inch gap), and cutting the food and harborage that drew them. Any baiting, where it is used at all, follows New Jersey's pesticide rules.

faqs.q: How is the price for a East Orange wildlife job figured?
faqs.a: By what the inspection finds: one squirrel entry at a gable vent is a short visit, while a raccoon family plus chewed fascia and fouled insulation is several. A two-family on a Greenwood street with one squirrel entry and a brick apartment house with a basement rat run are both East Orange inspections, and the line items are how the owner sees the difference. We walk the property with you, point out each opening, and price the removal, the sealing, and any cleanup as separate lines before work starts.

East Orange.wildlife_intro:
East Orange is dense, older, and built to last: brick apartment houses and substantial pre-war singles and twins on streets like those in the Ampere and Greenwood sections, many with slate or tile roofs and full masonry chimneys. Rats are the city's first wildlife problem, working the older basements, the shared sewer laterals, and the blocks behind the Main Street and Central Avenue food businesses. Raccoons den in the porch roofs and chimneys of the single-family streets, squirrels gnaw into the older eaves, and starlings occupy the signs and vents along the avenues.

Attached housing changes the math. In a rowhouse or twin, one animal in a shared attic or party-wall void is every neighbor's problem, and sealing a single unit while the adjoining roofline stays open just moves the tenant sideways. We inspect the whole run of connected rooflines where access allows, coordinate timing with neighbors when entries cross property lines, and seal the full set of openings under one plan. Older masonry party walls hide voids that let squirrels travel between houses unseen — finding those routes is most of the job in attached stock. East Orange's attached and apartment stock means a building's wildlife answer usually involves the whole structure's entries, and the quote says which ones belong to which owner.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Irvington?
faqs.a: It depends on the animal, how many entry points your home has, and how long the animals have been inside. Our crew inspects first, explains what we found, and gives you a quote after inspection before any removal or sealing work begins, with no prices promised over the phone.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Irvington chimney?
faqs.a: Yes — spring raccoon mothers choose uncapped chimneys across Essex County. Our crew checks whether pups are present before anything moves, removes the family together whenever we can, and fits a proper chimney cap so the same chimney is not a den again next spring.

faqs.q: Are squirrels in a Montclair attic actually a fire risk?
faqs.a: They can be. Squirrels gnaw constantly to wear their teeth, and wiring, PVC, and stored paper are all fair game; chewed conductors in a hot attic are a genuine hazard, not a sales line. In Montclair's oldest attics the wiring history is layered, and squirrel-gnawed runs are common enough that we photograph them as a matter of routine for the owner's electrician. Once the squirrels are out and the entries are meshed, we flag any chewed wiring we saw so an electrician can judge it — that check is part of why a squirrel job should never end at just closing the hole.

faqs.q: I found bat droppings in my Montclair attic — what happens next?
faqs.a: First we confirm the colony's size and find every entry, which is usually a cluster of small gaps at the ridge, a gable vent, or lifted flashing rather than one obvious hole. Upper Montclair's big attics are classic colony sites: high, hot, and entered at the ridge where the original roof meets a later dormer. Exclusion happens inside the NJ Fish & Wildlife guideline windows — April 1 to May 14 or August 1 to October 15 — using one-way exits, and the guano cleanup afterward is handled as a health material, bagged out rather than swept into the air.

Montclair.wildlife_intro:
Montclair is a town of big old houses on purpose: Victorians, Colonials, and Tudors climbing from Montclair Center through Watchung Plaza to Upper Montclair, with the First Watchung Mountain woods and Eagle Rock Reservation pressing on the west side. Deep lots, huge attics, and a century of additions give animals endless architecture. Squirrels and raccoons lead, entering at the junctions where additions meet original houses; bats hold colonies in the tall attics; groundhogs and skunks work the wooded west-side lots; and the whole town sits under a canopy that bridges straight to the rooflines.

Look at the trees before blaming the roof. A limb within jumping distance is a bridge, and squirrels treat overhanging branches the way people treat a front walk. Part of lasting proofing is arbor advice: limbs cut back several feet from the roofline, ivy stripped off walls where it gives climbers a ladder, and dense shrubs against the foundation thinned so animals lose their covered approach. Chimney and vent covers handle the rest. Houses under heavy canopy are never one-visit houses — the pressure is constant, so the sealing has to be thorough rather than quick. Montclair's canopy is the delivery system, so limb distance is measured and reported on every roofline inspection here, not treated as landscaping advice.

faqs.q: I hear scratching in my Bloomfield attic at night — what could it be?
faqs.a: Night scratching narrows the list: bats at dusk, flying squirrels gliding in after dark, raccoons moving heavily, or rats running a wall route. Daytime noise would point to gray squirrels instead. Brookdale's attics produce Bloomfield's night-noise calls, and flying squirrels, which glide in at the gable peaks in colonies, are the surprise answer more often than homeowners expect. Guessing wrong wastes money — the exits, timing, and sealing differ for each — so the inspection identifies the animal from droppings, entry size, and rub marks before any equipment is set.

faqs.q: We keep catching rats around our Bloomfield home — why do they come back?
faqs.a: Because the route and the restaurant are still open. Norway rats commute along fence lines, ivy, and utility runs, and they stay where trash, pet food, or a bird feeder feeds them every single night. Around Bloomfield Center the returns stop when the basement entries are mortared and the rear-yard food sources go; a trap-only visit in the older blocks has never once been the end of it. We map the runs, seal the building entries in metal and mortar — rats gnaw through foam and wood — and go over the sanitation changes that make the property stop paying out. Trapping alone, without those two halves, is a subscription, not a solution.

Bloomfield.wildlife_intro:
Bloomfield runs from the dense, older streets around Bloomfield Center and Watsessing up to Brookdale's postwar suburban blocks, and the wildlife changes with the housing. Near the center: rats in the older basements, raccoons in the porch roofs, starlings in the avenue signs. In Brookdale: squirrels in the colonial attics, skunks under the decks, groundhogs along the Third River and the golf-course edges. Halcyon Park and the older twins in between get both lists. The common thread is pre-war construction with a century of small gaps.

Most entries are not holes animals made — they are building failures animals found. Fascia boards rot behind gutters, soffit panels sag at the seams, and a gray squirrel needs only a small gap and one afternoon to widen it. Repairs here mean replacing the rotted wood, not just covering it, then backing vents and eave returns with metal that teeth cannot work through. Paint-matched covers keep the fix invisible from the street. Gutters clogged with leaf litter matter too: standing water softens the very boards that are supposed to keep animals out. Bloomfield's pre-war eaves are the recurring entry, and the repair here replaces the failed board rather than skinning it, because the next animal tests the same spot within the season.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my West Orange foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. On West Orange's slopes the burrow often starts in a terrace or wall and finishes under the house, which is why both entrances and the run between them get mapped before trapping starts. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

faqs.q: Can bats be evicted from my West Orange attic in the summer?
faqs.a: Not in midsummer. NJ Fish & Wildlife guidelines limit bat evictions to April 1 through May 14 and August 1 through October 15, because flightless pups would be trapped inside during the May 15 to July 31 maternity stretch. Slope homes under the reservation woods hold summer colonies most years, and a June discovery here means a documented plan and an August exclusion, with the living-space gaps sealed immediately so bats stay out of the bedrooms meanwhile. The work is exclusion only: one-way exits fitted during an open window, left in place through several mild nights, then every gap sealed once the colony has left. Bats are never trapped or killed — they are protected under the state's Endangered and Nongame Species Conservation Act.

West Orange.wildlife_intro:
West Orange climbs the Watchung slope from Pleasant Valley's older streets up through St. Cloud and Llewellyn Park to Eagle Rock Reservation, and the higher the street, the wilder the lot. Raccoons, skunks, and groundhogs work the wooded properties below the reservation; bats hold the attics of the older slope homes; squirrels are everywhere the oaks are. Llewellyn Park's historic houses, some of the oldest suburban homes in America, carry the same chimney-and-attic issues as any 1800s stock, with deer fencing and bear country at the top of the hill.

Yard damage tells its own story. Groundhog burrows throw fans of excavated soil against foundations, skunks leave neat cone-shaped holes hunting grubs, and moles push ridges and mounds across lawns that were level in April. Treating the yard means reading which animal made which sign — the remedies differ completely — and fixing the conditions underneath: grub-heavy turf, brush piles, and woodpiles stacked against the house. Burrows at foundations get backfilled and screened once the animals are out; a hole simply filled with dirt is a hole an animal reopens in a night. West Orange's terraced slope yards hide burrows in every retaining wall, so the ground survey here walks the walls and the lot's wood line, not just the foundation.

faqs.q: Moles are tearing up my Livingston yard — how are they handled?
faqs.a: By trapping the active runs, not by poison peanuts or vibrating stakes, which mostly rearrange the damage. Surface ridges are feeding tunnels; the deep runs along edges and foundations are the travel lanes where traps belong. Livingston lawns are watered and fed on schedule, which grows grubs on schedule, and the mole ridging follows the sprinkler pattern across the yard almost exactly. Eastern moles work most New Jersey lawns, and the star-nosed mole turns up in wetter ground. Expect a few visits spaced out — mole work is verified by fresh ridging stopping, not by a single day's catch.

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Livingston ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. The older capes here have low eaves a squirrel can reach from a fence or a woodpile, and the morning running usually starts at the corner nearest the trees. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

Livingston.wildlife_intro:
Livingston is a mature Essex suburb of capes and colonials from the postwar boom, now joined by large newer homes around Riker Hill and the Route 10 and Northfield corridors. The township kept its trees, and the Passaic River and the reservation edges keep wildlife in circulation. Squirrels and raccoons work the older capes' eaves and chimneys; groundhogs dig the bigger lots; moles ridge the irrigated lawns every spring; and bats pick off the quieter attics near the wooded pockets. It is preventable, detail-level work, mostly at soffits and vents.

Newer houses are not exempt — they just fail differently. Vinyl soffits flex and pop at the corners, roof-to-wall joints on additions open as materials settle, and bathroom vents often end in cheap plastic covers that starlings and squirrels push through in a season. Builders leave gaps around garage door corners and utility lines that rats and mice find within the first year. The work on a newer home is detail work: metal where plastic failed, backer rod and sealant at settling joints, and screens behind every vent cover rather than trust in the cover alone. Livingston's mix of 1950s capes and 1990s colonials means two different failure catalogs on the same street, and the inspection checklist here covers both.
